title: A Bid From a Dublin Bar and Digicel's First 100 Days in Jamaica
dek: In 2000 Denis O'Brien bought a Jamaican mobile licence his bankers warned him off, and in 2001 Digicel found far more customers than its own model allowed.

story.event: Bidding for a Jamaican mobile licence and launching Digicel against Cable & Wireless
story.summary: In 2000 a consortium led by Denis O'Brien, fresh from selling Esat, paid about $47.5 million at auction for one of two new mobile licences in Jamaica, where Cable & Wireless had long held the market and mobiles were seen as a luxury. Digicel launched in April 2001 with low prepaid rates, per-second billing and cheap or free handsets. By O'Brien's account it reached 100,000 subscribers in about 100 days, the number its own model had allowed for the whole first year, and soon overtook the incumbent.
paragraphs: One Friday evening in 2000, Denis O'Brien and a few colleagues followed an auction in Kingston, Jamaica, from Dublin, while their representative, Frank O'Carroll, bid in the room. "We bid from a bar in Dublin drinking rum," O'Brien later recalled. They won one of two new mobile licences, for about $47.5 million, a price he later called "the King's ransom."

O'Brien had just sold Esat, the Irish phone company he founded, to British Telecom, and had spotted the Jamaican government's tender in the Financial Times in late 1999. He said he asked only three questions: how many people lived in Jamaica, how many had phones, and how good the competition was. Cable & Wireless had dominated telephones in much of the Caribbean for more than a century. Mobiles cost $1 to $2 a minute for local calls and were seen as toys for the rich, and a landline could take two and a half years to install. His bankers advised against investing, and local partners reportedly declined, saying the incumbent was too entrenched.

He went ahead with former Esat colleagues, putting Seamus Lynch in charge in Kingston. Their own model put the outer limit of the market at 100,000 handsets in the first full year. Digicel launched on 19 April 2001 with 125 sites that it said covered over 80 per cent of the population. It charged less than half Cable & Wireless's rates, billed only for time actually used, and cut handset prices from about US$200 to US$20, or gave them away. Prepaid customers needed no fixed address, deposit or ID. "We just took the view that if you build a tower in the middle of nowhere, people will come," O'Brien said.

They came. Within about 100 days, by O'Brien's account, Digicel had 100,000 subscribers, the number its model had allowed for a whole year, and not long afterwards, he said, it overtook Cable & Wireless. Costs quickly ran past the US$100 million O'Brien had budgeted, and the company borrowed heavily to keep up with its growth. Jamaica became the template: by 2006 Digicel had taken the same approach to some 20 other Caribbean markets.

quote.text: Hence the stupidity and injustice of our opinions, so far as they deal with the significance of alien lives. Hence the falsity of our judgments, so far as they presume to decide in an absolute way on the value of other persons' conditions or ideals.
quote.work: Talks to Teachers on Psychology; and to Students on Some of Life's Ideals
quote.locator: Talks to Students, II: "On a Certain Blindness in Human Beings"
quote.source_title: Talks To Teachers On Psychology; And To Students On Some Of Life's Ideals, Project Gutenberg eBook #16287
quote.connection: James warns that we judge other people's lives from inside our own. Cable & Wireless treated mobiles as a luxury few Jamaicans wanted, and even Digicel's own model expected only 100,000 handsets in a year. The people who signed up had their own measure of what a phone was worth.

reflection: Most of us carry a quiet model of what other people want and what they can afford, built from our own lives. Cable & Wireless's model said mobiles were for the rich. Digicel's own, more generous, was still wrong by a wide margin. What corrected it was not a better spreadsheet but putting something in front of people and seeing what they did.

You will have assumptions like these about the people you hope to serve, and about the people closest to you: what they would pay for, what they would use, what they would welcome. Some will be right. The ones worth testing first are those you have never checked with the person concerned.
invitation: Pick one assumption you hold about what someone else wants, whether a colleague, a customer or someone at home. Ask them directly today, in one plain question, and listen to the whole answer.

research_notes: First-year expectations disagree within and between sources. The Jamaica Observer (2010) says O'Brien, Lynch and Smith built a model putting the outer limit at 100,000 handsets for the first full year, but also quotes O'Brien that 'it would be wonderful to get to 300,000 customers' and that the first year's target was surpassed within months. In USA Today (2006) O'Brien says 100,000 subscribers within 100 days. The story uses the 100,000 model and gives the 100-day figure as O'Brien's claim; no operator or regulator figure was found. Overtaking Cable & Wireless: USA Today has O'Brien saying 'eleven months later' (unclear whether after launch or after the first 100 days); the story says only 'not long afterwards, he said'. Licence: the Irish Times (2005) says it was bought at auction on a Friday evening in April 2000; RTÉ (2001) says the licence was won in June 2000; both give $47.5 million (the Observer says US$47 million). The story says 'in 2000'. Where O'Brien was: the Observer quotes 'a bar in Dublin'; the Irish Times says the Morrison Hotel in Dublin; the story says only that they followed from Dublin. Investment: the Observer says O'Brien budgeted US$100 million and costs quickly surpassed it; RTÉ at launch gave $180 million total; RCR Wireless (September 2001) over US$177 million; the Irish Times $150 million initial by the consortium's account. The story uses only O'Brien's planned figure, attributed. Pre-Digicel mobile penetration: USA Today 4% in 2001, RTÉ 7%, the Irish Times about 10% (270,000 users); not used. Funding is 'mixed': O'Brien's Esat proceeds with heavy borrowing. The company field names Mossel (Jamaica), the consortium company that launched the Digicel brand. Moriarty Tribunal: not mentioned, as the story keeps to the 2000-01 Jamaica launch. William James's essay is about judging other people's inner lives; it is applied by analogy.
